questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish selection from chance change in allele frequency
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-101 asks which observation best demonstrates that a trait is subject to natural selection rather than drifting by chance.

options.text: The trait is present in the population and its frequency has remained steady for many years
options.misconception: treats steady frequency as proof of an active selective force

options.text: The trait appears only in individuals that feed at the edge of the reef where food is scarce
options.misconception: links a trait to habitat without linking it to survival

options.text: Individuals with the trait survive better and leave more offspring when the condition changes
The trait is physically larger than the alternative form in most members of the population
options.misconception: confuses physical size with reproductive advantage

questions.explanation: Selection is identified by a survival or reproduction difference tied to the trait, so carriers must leave more descendants when conditions change. Mere stability, habitat alone or mere size fit chance too.
questions.hint: Look for a difference in offspring produced.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a new allele in one person does not disturb equilibrium
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-106 asks for an explanation of why a newly detected allele in one patient is not evidence against Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

answer.exemplar: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes a population in which allele and genotype frequencies stay stable across generations because no evolutionary force is acting on it. A single new allele in one individual does not disturb that population-level balance, since the model concerns allele and genotype frequencies in whole populations over many generations. Rare mutations do occur, and they are what evolution ultimately depends on, but their appearance in one patient is a microscopic event rather than a change in the equilibrium of the population.

questions.explanation: The model assumes a large population, random mating and no selection or mutation, and describes allele frequencies across generations. One new allele in one person is far too rare to shift that.
questions.hint: Think about population level rather than individual level.

questions.stem: A population of 200 individuals contains 50 heterozygotes and 150 homozygotes for a trait. Heterozygotes have relative fitness 1.0 and homozygotes 0.5. After selection, what fraction of the survivors will be heterozygotes?
questions.explanation: Survivors number 50 times 1.0 plus 150 times 0.5, which is 125, and 50 of 125 is 0.4. Selection raised the heterozygote share because homozygotes left fewer survivors.
questions.hint: Weight each genotype by its fitness first.

options.misconception: confuses size with growth rate in the model

options.misconception: claims population size controls how mating happens

options.text: In a large population chance sampling error is negligible, so frequencies are not moved by accident

options.misconception: believes selection is too weak to act on rare variants

options.misconception: proposes a different measurement as the correction

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how antibiotic resistance supports the theory of evolution
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-114 asks for a short explanation of why antibiotic resistance in bacteria counts as evidence for evolution.

answer.exemplar: Antibiotic resistance is evidence for evolution because the resistant lineages were not present in the same form before the drug was used; resistant variants already existed at low frequency or arose by mutation, and selection by the antibiotic favoured them, so their frequency rose steeply. In the same way that beak shape in finches tracks the availability of food, the antibiotic response tracks the pressure imposed by treatment, and the laboratory can observe both the selection and the outcome.

questions.explanation: Selection by an antibiotic acts on variation already present or arising by mutation, so resistant forms increase in frequency while the drug is used, as in other documented cases of evolution.
questions.hint: Link the change in frequency to the selective pressure.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Contrast selection with random change in allele frequency
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-122 asks for an explanation of how natural selection differs from a random change in allele frequency.

answer.exemplar: Natural selection is non-random with respect to phenotype: individuals with traits that suit the current conditions leave more offspring, so the alleles behind those traits become more common. A random change in allele frequency, by contrast, depends only on chance events such as sampling error, and does not depend on how well an organism is adapted. The test is whether the change tracks the trait and its advantage, or merely tracks the size of the population.

questions.explanation: Natural selection requires a heritable difference affecting reproductive success, so the fitter phenotype contributes more descendants. Drift also shifts frequencies but is not tied to the trait.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change depends on the trait's advantage.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the conditions assumed by the Hardy-Weinberg model
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-130 asks for a paragraph explaining what the Hardy-Weinberg conditions represent and why they matter.

answer.exemplar: The Hardy-Weinberg conditions are a checklist of assumptions under which allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation: a very large population so sampling error is negligible, random mating so genotypes are shuffled evenly, no mutation adding or removing alleles, no migration bringing alleles in, and no selection favouring one genotype. They are a null model rather than a description of most real populations, and a population that departs from them is one where an evolutionary force is acting.

questions.explanation: The conditions describe a population where nothing favours one allele and chance sampling is negligible. Real populations break at least one, and which one fails shows the evolutionary force at work.
questions.hint: Think about what the model assumes rather than what it predicts.

options.misconception: claims large size rules out all genetic drift

options.text: The population is mixed, so the random mating condition is certainly satisfied
options.misconception: assumes a mixed population guarantees random mating

options.text: Every individual was genotyped, so the frequencies cannot be wrong
options.misconception: believes complete genotyping removes the need to test assumptions

options.text: Measured genotype frequencies differ significantly from p squared, 2pq and q squared, so a force is acting

questions.explanation: Departure from expected genotype proportions is what the model is designed to detect, and it points to selection, migration, non-random mating or drift. Sample size alone proves nothing.
questions.hint: Compare measured and expected genotype proportions.

options.misconception: links selectability to how fast a trait changes

Because behaviour is always the result of an individual's own learning and never of genes

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an inherited trait from one acquired during life

options.misconception: treats one family resemblance as proof of genetic inheritance

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fossils and DNA together support common ancestry
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-138 asks for a paragraph explaining why fossils and DNA from living species both support common ancestry.

answer.exemplar: Fossils document ancestral forms in dated rock layers and show that the sequence of forms matches the order in which the living species are nested by DNA similarity. Molecular sequences add a second, independent line: mutations accumulate steadily, so related species carry fewer differences, and the branching pattern of those differences matches the branching pattern drawn from anatomy and from the fossil record. Neither record stands alone, but the agreement of three independent approaches is what makes common ancestry compelling.

questions.explanation: Fossils place ancestral forms in a dated sequence, and molecular changes accumulate steadily so close relatives share fewer. Agreement between independent evidence makes common ancestry well supported.
questions.hint: Think about two independent kinds of record.

questions.explanation: The homozygous recessive frequency is q squared, which is 0.09, and 0.09 of 2000 is 180. Using 0.3 directly gives 600, which counts carriers too.
questions.hint: Square the frequency before multiplying by the population.

options.misconception: invents a slow-change rule for structures

options.misconception: believes recessive alleles are always visible in every copy

options.text: The recessive allele becomes rarer, but slowly, since it is hidden from selection in heterozygotes
The recessive allele becomes commoner because carriers are protected from the selection
options.misconception: reverses the direction of selection on the allele

options.text: The allele frequency stays the same, because selection only affects the dominant phenotype
options.misconception: assumes selection cannot see recessive homozygotes

questions.explanation: Selection removes homozygotes, but heterozygotes carry the allele while showing the dominant phenotype, so it declines only gradually and is never removed entirely by selection alone.

options.text: The frequency rose because resistant cells were counted twice in the final measurement
options.misconception: invokes a counting error with no evidence

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct an allele frequency pair that cannot describe a population
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-145 reports that a laboratory calculated allele frequencies of p equal to 0.6 and q equal to 0.6 for a population and then used them to predict genotype proportions.

options.text: The calculation is sound, because the two alleles need not have complementary frequencies
options.misconception: misses that the two allele frequencies must sum to one

options.text: The calculation is sound, because Hardy-Weinberg proportions allow any allele frequencies
options.misconception: ignores the constraint between p and q

options.text: Allele frequencies must sum to one, so q should be 0.4 and every predicted count must be recalculated
The calculation is sound, because genotype frequencies depend only on the number of samples
options.misconception: claims sample size sets genotype proportions

questions.explanation: The two allele frequencies are complementary, so p plus q is one and q here must be 0.4. Predictions made from values that do not sum to one describe no real population.
questions.hint: Check that the two allele frequencies add to one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a resistant strain spreads through a hospital population
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-146 asks for an explanation of how a drug-resistant strain can spread through a hospital population.

answer.exemplar: A resistant strain spreads because antibiotic use is a selection pressure: cells carrying a resistance mechanism, whether from a plasmid or a mutation, survive treatment while susceptible cells do not, so the survivors reproduce and the resistance allele rises in frequency in each treated patient. Selection acts on the phenotype, so the mechanism need not be identical in every patient, which is why resistance emerges repeatedly in wards where antibiotics are used heavily.

questions.explanation: Treatment kills susceptible cells and leaves resistant ones, so resistant variants are favoured and become common. Selection acts on the mechanism present in each case.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the two groups during treatment.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the link between allele and genotype frequencies
questions.stem: Clinician's note CN-154 asks for an explanation of how allele and genotype frequencies are related under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

answer.exemplar: Allele frequency describes how the copies of a gene are distributed between variants, while genotype frequency describes how those copies are paired into individuals. Under Hardy-Weinberg conditions the two are linked by a simple rule: with p the frequency of one allele and q the frequency of the other, the homozygous genotypes occur at p squared and q squared and the heterozygous genotype at 2pq, and because p plus q equals one, the three frequencies sum to one. That gives expected counts for any population large enough to ignore sampling error.

questions.explanation: Under equilibrium genotype frequencies are p squared, 2pq and q squared, and since p plus q is one the three must total one. A different total shows the assumptions are broken.
questions.hint: Think about how allele copies are paired into genotypes.
